A good home inspector is worth their weight in gold, but don't just trust your real estate agent's suggestion. If at all possible, follow the inspector around as he can verbally identify potential issues that may not all make it into the final report that you'll want to remedy soon after you take possession/move into the house.

The real estate agent works for the seller, so be careful how much you tell them. While not perfect, it may be worth watching a few buying a home shows on HG to learn common agent tactics (getting your upper limit then using that to push you toward/away from the homes they show).

If in the US, be cautious about homes built between 2004 and 2008, especially later in that range, as at some point in there, builders realized the party was ending and had immense pressure to take short cuts to get this project sold.

Read carefully the covenants of the HOA if it applies to a home, know that you will be comfortable with their rules (as HOAs tend to attract petty tyrants so violations are quickly punished).

The real estate agent works for the seller, so be careful how much you tell them.

I disagree. The real estate agent works for their commission. There is no incentive for them to get the most for the seller because a $10-20k difference in price doesn't affect their commission very much. All they want to do is make the sale.

What you need to watch out for is real estate agents pushing their listings on you. If they sell one of their listed properties, they don't have to split commissions with another agents. The very first time I went house hunting the agent I was working with kept showing me crap properties that didn't fit what I was asking for (this was before the MLS and being able to easily browse properties online). I ended up ditching him and going with someone else. I realized later the first agent only showed me things he listed.

Bottom line, do not trust the real estate agent. At the end of the day they don't have your best interest in mind. You can use their advice and knowledge of the market, but ALWAYS read between the lines. They will sugar coat everything.

The last two houses I bought, I pretty much only used the agent to get access to the properties and push paperwork. I researched the properties online and told them what I wanted to look at.

Read carefully the covenants of the HOA if it applies to a home, know that you will be comfortable with their rules (as HOAs tend to attract petty tyrants so violations are quickly punished).

Also usually unenforceable. The only HOA I knew which was even sort of enforceable was one that a service buddy took out in Oklahoma . They basically knew they had those guys over a barrel for not being able to work on their houses while doing military stuff and they knew that they had to live close to base. Combined with a teaser offer for Community Association Banking, the HOA and all its fines were rolled into the mortgage.

Avoid that at all costs, the HOA has no power whatsoever if they can't get at your money before you can.
In 20 states, they can put a senior lien on your property which allows them to eventually foreclose, or at the least make a resale at some point quite difficult.
For us, an HOA was an automatic deal breaker.

That I should go on the home inspection.

With my first house, I wasn't really given the option as my Realtor (who ended up being a really shady individual) booked the inspection and told me it would be finished by a particular date. She pushed the idea it was only for the bank and not much for me. I didn't even consider the possibilities of home inspections raising red flags.

I've bought two homes since then. I've gone on both inspections and had conversations with the inspector. The inspector isn't allowed to do some things - like move something out of the way to look behind it. I think it is an insurance thing. I, on the other hand, can. I can make things accessible to the inspector that he would normally have to shrug off. A good example - one of the houses I looked at had an attic entrance in one of the bedrooms. There was a wardrobe directly under it blocking access. The inspector couldn't move it, so I did.

In both cases, the things the inspector found weren't deal breakers, but there were things that needed fixed that I missed. This allowed me to go back to the seller, point out the few things that needed repaired, and adjust my offer to account for it. In both cases, my offer was accepted at the lower rate.
